title: Towards fifty
objectives: Find which operation costs you the most time and drill it.

screens.title: Two targets
screens.prose: This course trains two targets. The first is the daily warm-up on Today, a Zetamac round: 120 seconds of mixed questions on Zetamac's default settings. Stage 0 asked for a score of 25, which is 4.8 seconds an answer. Stage 3 and the topic exit ask for 50.
screens.question: How many seconds an answer does a score of 50 allow?

hints.text: Share the 120 seconds among 50 answers.
Doubling the score halves the time each answer gets.

feedback.correct: $120 \div 50 = 2.4$ seconds an answer, half the Stage 0 pace.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the 120 seconds by the 50 answers.

byKey.flipped: $50 \div 120$ is answers per second. The question asks for seconds per answer.
byKey.gap: 70 is $120 - 50$. Divide the time by the number of answers instead.
byKey.stage0: 4.8 seconds is the pace for 25. A score of 50 needs twice as many answers.

explain.text: Fifty answers share 120 seconds, so each gets $120 \div 50 = 2.4$ seconds. That is half the Stage 0 pace of 4.8 seconds.

screens.prose: Drag the point to set a pace. The caption gives the score that pace reaches in 120 seconds. Watch how little the point moves near the fast end.

derive.caption: {{fixed(s.x, 1)}} seconds an answer: a score of {{floor(120 / s.x + 0.0001)}}

screens.question: How many seconds an answer separate a score of 40 from a score of 50?

hints.text: Find the pace for 40, then the pace for 50.
Drag the point to 3.0, then to 2.4.
$120 \div 40 = 3$ and $120 \div 50 = 2.4$, so the gap is 0.6 seconds.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out both paces, then subtract.

byKey.points: 10 is the gap in score. The question asks for the gap in seconds an answer.
byKey.fifty: 2.4 seconds is the pace for 50 itself. Subtract it from the pace for 40.
byKey.forty: 3 seconds is the pace for 40 itself. Subtract the pace for 50 from it.

explain.text: A score of 40 needs 3 seconds an answer and 50 needs 2.4. From 30 to 40 costs a whole second; from 40 to 50 only 0.6. Near 50, each tenth of a second you save is worth about two points.

screens.title: The second target
screens.prose: The second target is the 80-in-8 arithmetic test set by some trading firms. As reported in 2026, it has 80 four-option questions in 8 minutes and no skipping. It scores +1 right and −1 wrong. About 55 net is the reported mark.

rows: 80 four-option items in 480 s, +1 right, −1 wrong

screens.question: You answer 64 questions and 5 of them are wrong. What is your net score?

hints.text: Net is right answers minus wrong answers.
64 answered with 5 wrong leaves 59 right.

feedback.correct: 59 right minus 5 wrong is 54, one short of the reported mark.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the right answers, then take off one point for each wrong one.

byKey.right-only: You counted the 59 right answers but did not take off the 5 wrong ones.
byKey.answered: 64 is every answer given. Five of them were wrong and each costs a point.
byKey.wrong-only: You kept only the penalty. The 59 right answers earn a point each.

explain.text: 59 right minus 5 wrong is 54. A wrong answer costs two points against a right one: one lost and one not earned. At 6 seconds a question, accuracy matters as much as pace.

screens.title: A candidate's round
screens.prose: A candidate logged one warm-up round, seeded: 30 answers, then the bell cut off a 31st after 4.5 seconds. “wrong” means the first answer typed was wrong, so the question waited for a second try. The totals per operation are below.
screens.question: Fill in the mean seconds for each operation, to 2 decimal places.

hints.text: A mean is the total seconds divided by the number of answers.
Division: $56.2 \div 10$. The division rows are highlighted.

feedback.correct: 2.41, 2.53, 3.6 and 5.62 seconds. Division is more than twice as slow as addition.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide each total by its number of answers.

byKey.r0c2: $19.3 \div 8$: 16 goes once, and 3.3 left is about 0.41. So 2.41.
byKey.r1c2: $7.6 \div 3$: 6 gives 2, and 1.6 left is about 0.53. So 2.53.
byKey.r3c2: $56.2 \div 10$ moves the point one place: 5.62. Divide the seconds by the answers, not the other way.

explain.text: Each mean is the total time over the count. Division averages 5.62 seconds, more than twice addition’s 2.41. The ten divisions took 56.2 of the 115.5 seconds used.

screens.prose: You sorted a round by operation to find where its time went. That is **error analysis**: which kind is slow, which is wrong, and why. Here are your means as bars.
screens.question: What share of the 115.5 seconds went on division, to the nearest whole per cent?

hints.text: Division took 56.2 seconds in total.
Share of time is $56.2 \div 115.5$.
$115.5 \times 0.5 = 57.75$, a little more than 56.2. So the share is just under 50%: about 49%.

feedback.correct: $56.2 \div 115.5 = 0.487$, about 49%. A third of the answers took half the time.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide division’s total seconds by the seconds used.

byKey.count: 10 of 30 answers is a third of the questions. The question asks for the share of the time.
byKey.mean-share: You compared the four means. A share of time comes from the totals: 56.2 of 115.5.

explain.text: A third of the questions took almost half the round, so division is where the score is. The **drill rule**: drill the slowest operation on its own, then go back to mixed rounds. For many candidates the slowest kind is division, or multiplications such as $7 \times 64$.

screens.prose: A simpler candidate: divisions take 6 seconds and the other three kinds 2 seconds each. The warm-up on Today picks each kind equally often, so a quarter of the questions are divisions.
screens.question: What is the round's mean pace, in seconds an answer?

hints.text: Weight each time by its share of the questions.
Divisions add $0.25 \times 6 = 1.5$ seconds to the mean.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Weight each kind’s seconds by its share, then add.

byKey.two-kinds: You averaged 6 and 2 as if half the questions were divisions. Only a quarter are.
byKey.ignore: 2 seconds leaves out the divisions. They are a quarter of the round.
byKey.sum: 12 is the four times added. Weight each one by its share of a quarter.

explain.text: A quarter of the questions at 6 seconds and three quarters at 2 average to 3 seconds. That pace gives $120 \div 3 = 40$. One slow kind drags the whole round down.

screens.prose: A week of division drill takes the same candidate from 6 seconds to 3. The other kinds stay at 2 seconds.
screens.question: What score does the new pace give? A score counts whole answers, so round down.

hints.text: Find the new pace first, then divide 120 by it.
The pace is $0.25 \times 3 + 0.75 \times 2 = 2.25$ seconds.
$120 \div 2.25 = 53.3$, so 53 whole answers.

feedback.correct: A pace of 2.25 seconds gives $120 \div 2.25 = 53.3$, so 53. Halving one kind lifted the score by 13.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Weight the new times by their shares, then divide 120 by the pace.

byKey.ignore: 60 is $120 \div 2$, as if divisions took 2 seconds too. They take 3.
byKey.unweighted: You averaged 3 and 2 equally. Divisions are only a quarter of the questions.
byKey.old: 40 was the score before the drill. Divisions now take 3 seconds, not 6.
byKey.pace: 2.25 seconds is the pace. The score is 120 divided by it.

explain.text: Divisions now add $0.25 \times 3 = 0.75$ seconds to the mean, not 1.5. The pace drops to 2.25 seconds and the score passes 50. No other kind changed.

screens.prose: Two candidates start at 6 seconds for division and 2 for the rest. Each cuts one kind by a fifth in a week. Ana drills addition, which she enjoys: 2.0 to 1.6 seconds. Ben drills division: 6.0 to 4.8 seconds.
screens.question: Who scores more next week?

options.text: Ben: there was more time to cut
Ana: she practised the kind she does best
options.why: You picked the drill that feels good. A fifth off 2 seconds saves 0.4; a fifth off 6 saves 1.2.

options.text: Level: both cut their time by a fifth
options.why: A fifth of a big time is more seconds than a fifth of a small one: 1.2 against 0.4.

options.text: Ana: additions come up more often
options.why: In the warm-up each kind comes up a quarter of the time. Additions are not more common.

hints.text: Work out each candidate’s new pace.
Ana: $0.25 \times 6 + 0.25 \times 1.6 + 0.5 \times 2 = 2.9$ seconds.

feedback.correct: Ben’s pace is 2.7 seconds, a score of 44. Ana’s is 2.9, a score of 41.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out both new paces, then divide 120 by each.

byKey.ana: You picked the drill that feels good. A fifth off 2 seconds saves 0.4; a fifth off 6 saves 1.2.
byKey.level: A fifth of a big time is more seconds than a fifth of a small one: 1.2 against 0.4.
byKey.often: In the warm-up each kind comes up a quarter of the time. Additions are not more common.

explain.text: Ana saved $0.25 \times 0.4 = 0.1$ seconds a question on average, and Ben $0.25 \times 1.2 = 0.3$. Practising what is already fast feels like progress but moves the score little.

screens.prose: You weighted each kind’s time by its share, then divided 120 by the result. $$\bar t = \sum_k w_k t_k, \qquad \text{score} = \left\lfloor \frac{120}{\bar t} \right\rfloor$$ Here $w_k$ is kind $k$’s share of the questions and $t_k$ its mean seconds.
screens.question: Divisions take 7 seconds and the rest 2, a quarter each: a score of 36. Which single change lifts the score most?

options.text: Divisions down to 5 seconds: a score of 43
All three fast kinds down to 1.5 seconds: a score of 41
options.why: Three kinds 0.5 seconds faster save $0.75 \times 0.5 = 0.375$ seconds a question. Divisions 2 seconds faster save 0.5.

options.text: Additions down to 1 second: a score of 40
options.why: Halving addition saves $0.25 \times 1 = 0.25$ seconds a question. Divisions 2 seconds faster save 0.5.

feedback.correct: Divisions at 5 seconds give a pace of 2.75 and a score of 43.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out the saving per question: share times seconds saved.

explain.text: The saving per question is the share times the seconds saved. Divisions save $0.25 \times 2 = 0.5$, the three fast kinds $0.75 \times 0.5 = 0.375$, addition alone 0.25. The biggest saving gives the biggest score.

screens.prose: Now work backwards from a target. The other kinds hold at 2 seconds, and divisions are a quarter of the questions. How fast must division be for a score of 50? Put the working in order, and leave out the line that does not belong.
screens.question: Put the lines in order.

lines.text: A score of 50 needs a pace of $120 \div 50 = 2.4$ seconds, from the score rule
$0.25\,d + 0.75 \times 2 = 2.4$, the weighted mean with divisions at $d$ seconds
$0.25\,d = 2.4 - 1.5 = 0.9$, take off the three fast kinds’ share
$d = 2.4 \times 4 = 9.6$ seconds, all the pace goes on division
lines.why: You gave all 2.4 seconds to division. The other three quarters of the questions use 1.5 of them.

hints.text: Which line turns the score into a pace?
The weighted mean comes next, with $d$ unknown.

feedback.correct: Divisions at 3.6 seconds, with the rest at 2, give a score of exactly 50.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start from the pace the score needs.

byKey.all: You gave all 2.4 seconds to division. The other three quarters of the questions use 1.5 of them.
byKey.left-out: Every line except the 9.6-second one belongs in the working.
byKey.mix: The weighted mean needs the target pace first.
byKey.take: Take off the fast kinds only once the weighted mean is written.
byKey.solve: Solving for $d$ is the last step.

explain.text: The score rule turns 50 into a pace of 2.4 seconds. Three quarters of the questions at 2 seconds use 1.5 of it, leaving 0.9 for the quarter that are divisions. So each division may take $0.9 \times 4 = 3.6$ seconds.

screens.title: Let Python sort the log
screens.prose: Each log entry is `(question, op, seconds, first_try_right)`, with `op` one of `'add'`, `'sub'`, `'mul'` and `'div'`. `LOG` holds the round you analysed, already defined.
screens.question: Complete `seconds_by_op(log)`, a dict of mean seconds per operation, and `slowest(log)`, the operation with the largest mean.

tests.call: {k: round(v, 4) for k, v in seconds_by_op(LOG).items()}
round(sum(seconds_by_op(LOG)[k] * n for k, n in [('add', 8), ('sub', 3), ('mul', 9), ('div', 10)]), 4)

widget.how: Check runs 7 hidden tests on `LOG` and on short logs. Means are rounded to 4 places and compared exactly. An operation missing from a log is missing from the dict.

hints.text: Use `dict.get(op, 0)` to start a total at zero.
`totals[op] = totals.get(op, 0) + seconds`, and the same with 1 for the count. Division should come out at 5.62.
`max(means, key=means.get)` returns the key with the largest value.

feedback.correct: Division, at 5.62 seconds, is the slowest kind in `LOG`.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the totals and counts are both updated in the loop.

explain.text: The loop builds a total and a count per operation, and the dict comprehension divides them. `max` with `key=means.get` compares the means but returns the operation. Run it on your own logged round to find your drill.

screens.prose: Your online test for a trading firm is in two weeks. Your own warm-up log looks like the candidate’s: division is slowest. The daily warm-up on Today suggests five rounds, about 10 minutes. You have 15 minutes a day.
screens.question: Which plan follows the drill rule and shows whether it worked?

options.text: Each day: 5 minutes of divisions alone, then five warm-up rounds; compare this week’s average score with last week’s
Each day: 15 minutes of warm-up rounds, judged by the best score
options.why: Mixed rounds give division only a quarter of your practice. A best score is one lucky round, not a trend.

options.text: All week: divisions only, with no mixed rounds
options.why: Drill the slow kind alone, then mix again. The test is mixed, so switching between kinds needs practice too.

options.text: Each day: 5 minutes of additions, then five warm-up rounds
options.why: Addition is already your fastest kind. Practising it feels good but moves the score least.

hints.text: The drill rule has two parts.
Drill the slowest kind on its own, then mix.
And one round is noisy: the warm-up chart shows your last ten for that reason.

feedback.correct: Drill division alone, keep the mixed rounds, and judge by the average of many rounds.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for the slow kind drilled alone, then mixed rounds, then a fair test of progress.

byKey.rounds: Mixed rounds give division only a quarter of your practice. A best score is one lucky round, not a trend.
byKey.only: Drill the slow kind alone, then mix again. The test is mixed, so switching between kinds needs practice too.
byKey.adds: Addition is already your fastest kind. Practising it feels good but moves the score least.

explain.text: Five minutes of divisions targets the kind that costs most, and the five rounds keep the mix. The warm-up’s chart shows your last ten rounds, so an average, not one score, tells you it worked. Note each score from Today in your log.

ideas: Pace is seconds per answer: a score of 50 in 120 seconds needs 2.4 seconds an answer.
A round’s pace is each kind’s time weighted by its share. One slow kind drags the score down.
Drill the slowest kind alone, then mix again, and judge progress by many rounds, not one.

quiz.prose: Your multiplications by 10 take 2 seconds when the first try is right. One first try in four is wrong, and each wrong try costs 3 more seconds before you notice and retype.

feedback.correct: $2 + 0.25 \times 3 = 2.75$ seconds. A fast kind that is often wrong is not fast.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the expected cost of the wrong tries.

explain.text: Each question costs 2 seconds, plus 3 seconds a quarter of the time. That adds $0.25 \times 3 = 0.75$ seconds. In the warm-up a wrong answer simply waits, so slips cost time.

explain.text: A score of 40 needs a pace of $120 \div 40 = 3$ seconds. The fast kinds use $0.75 \times 2.5 = 1.875$, leaving 1.125 for the divisions’ quarter. So $d = 1.125 \times 4 = 4.5$ seconds.
